title: Oracle Projects Cash Flow Positive by 2028; Stock Soars on Bullish Outlook
body:
Oracle Corp. signaled a dramatic turnaround in its financial outlook on Tuesday, projecting that it will generate positive cash flow by 2028 and forecasting fiscal‑2030 revenue of more than $225 billion. The guidance topped Wall Street consensus, which had expected $217.7 billion, and sent the company’s shares sharply higher in after‑hours trading. The upbeat outlook comes as the broader tech sector grapples with mixed earnings, highlighted by Alphabet’s steepest one‑day slide in over six years and Microsoft’s robust results that lifted its own stock.

The software giant’s new cash‑flow target reflects a strategic pivot that began with the 2022 acquisition of Cerner, a move that broadened Oracle’s footprint in the lucrative health‑care data market. Executives say the integration of Cerner’s electronic‑health‑record platform, combined with a push to modernize legacy on‑premises offerings through cloud‑first initiatives, is now delivering the scale needed to offset a historically heavy reliance on licensing fees. “We are seeing the momentum from our cloud‑infrastructure services and industry‑specific SaaS solutions converge, creating a more resilient revenue mix,” said Oracle’s CFO during the earnings call.

Analysts note that the $225 billion revenue projection represents a compound annual growth rate of roughly 8 % from the company’s 2023 earnings of $125 billion, a pace that outstrips most of its enterprise‑software peers. The optimism is underpinned by several growth vectors: continued expansion of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) in the Asia‑Pacific region, deeper penetration into the financial‑services sector with its autonomous database, and the rollout of AI‑enhanced applications that leverage the firm’s vast data assets. Moreover, Oracle’s recent partnership with Nvidia to embed generative‑AI capabilities into its cloud stack is expected to attract high‑margin workloads that traditionally gravitate toward competitors such as Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure.

The market reaction was swift. Oracle’s stock jumped more than 7 % in extended trading, erasing a modest decline it had endured earlier in the week amid broader tech volatility. By contrast, Alphabet (Google’s parent) posted earnings that missed revenue expectations, prompting its shares to tumble 12 %—the steepest decline since 2017. Microsoft, meanwhile, posted a beat‑and‑raise, with its cloud and AI segments delivering record growth, lifting its shares 5 % in pre‑market activity. The divergent performances underscore a sector in transition, where firms that successfully blend cloud infrastructure with AI‑driven services are reaping premium valuations, while those slower to adapt face heightened investor scrutiny.

Investors are also weighing Oracle’s capital allocation plan. The company announced a $10 billion share‑repurchase program and a modest dividend increase, signaling confidence in its cash‑generation capacity. Yet, skeptics point to the lingering risk of legacy contract renewals and the competitive pressure from hyperscale cloud providers that enjoy deeper ecosystems and broader developer communities. The firm’s ability to sustain its projected cash flow hinges on converting a larger share of its existing enterprise customer base to subscription‑based models and capturing new business in fast‑growing verticals such as health‑care, government, and fintech.

Looking ahead, Oracle’s roadmap suggests that the next few years will be pivotal. If the firm can maintain its revenue trajectory and achieve cash‑flow positivity by 2028, it could position itself as a credible third‑tier cloud contender, narrowing the gap with Amazon, Microsoft, and Google. Such a shift would not only bolster shareholder returns but also reshape the competitive dynamics of the enterprise‑software market. For now, the market’s upbeat response reflects a cautious optimism that Oracle’s strategic bets are beginning to pay off, setting the stage for a potentially transformative decade for the long‑standing tech stalwart.
